project.title: Cognitive Bias Ontology
project.description: Sixteen OWL ontologies of cognitive biases, and an explorer that walks through each user story as a graph and tests every competency question with SPARQL.
project.introText: An ontology for a cluster of cognitive biases, part of a collective ontology of human biases built by the whole class of Knowledge Representation and Extraction (prof. Aldo Gangemi, University of Bologna, 2022/23).

gridImages.caption: The Gambler's Fallacy ontology drawn from its OWL file: the lottery user story as individuals and relations, with each class marked by where it comes from.
Story walk: the Gambler's Fallacy user story sentence by sentence; the individuals each sentence describes are outlined, the ones not yet reached are faint.

A competency question tested: the fixed query runs in the browser and its answer, the recent memory, is marked on the graph. The GitBook's own query asked for the inverse property and returned nothing.
Gambler's fallacy and the hot-hand fallacy side by side: mirror-image biases, with the classes and properties both models use marked in each.
Reuse matrix: which design patterns and Framester frames each of the 16 ontologies actually uses in its user-story graph, and which it only documents.
Filtering by design pattern: selecting Affected By picks out the seven ontologies whose user stories are built on it.

project.middleText: Our group, Marco Lamorte, Corrado Consiglio, Salvatore Di Marzo and I, modeled sixteen biases, from the gambler's fallacy and the hot hand fallacy to pareidolia, naive realism and the blind spot bias. Each went through the same eXtreme Design workflow: research and documentation, ideation and design, modeling and implementation, then presentation and visualization. ChatGPT and Gemini were used early on for definitions, scenarios and user stories, and Framester among the resources for modeling.
project.conclusionText: The process is documented in a public GitBook. It showed how much understanding of a domain an ontology needs before any modeling starts, and where language models help and where their answers had to be corrected. In 2026 I built an explorer on the group's OWL files: it walks through each user story sentence by sentence as the graph fills in, compares any two ontologies, and runs every competency question as SPARQL in the browser. Testing showed what the documentation did not: only 12 of the group's 24 written queries answered their question as written, mostly because of reversed properties and typos. Fixed and completed, 37 of the 47 questions are answered by the files, 7 in part, and 3 ask about things the files do not record.
project.highlightCaption: The explorer's overview: 16 ontologies, 119 classes, 52 object properties and 121 user-story assertions.
project.context: Knowledge Representation and Extraction (prof. Aldo Gangemi), 2022/23, MA Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge, University of Bologna
project.reworkNote: The ontologies were built as a group project with Marco Lamorte, Corrado Consiglio and Salvatore Di Marzo for Knowledge Representation and Extraction (2022/23). In 2026 I independently built a visual explorer from the group's OWL files and documentation, and tested every competency question against them; the images here come from it.

summary.brief: Cognitive biases are described in prose; there was no shared formal model to query them.
summary.role: Four of the sixteen ontologies (bias blind spot, confabulation, naive cynicism and naive realism), in a team of four; the 2026 explorer on my own.
summary.method: eXtreme Design: user stories, competency questions, ontology design patterns and alignment to Framester; in 2026, every competency question tested as SPARQL.
summary.outcome: 16 OWL ontologies (119 classes, 52 object properties) and an explorer that walks through each story and tests all 47 competency questions: 37 are answered by the files.
summary.stack: OWL, RDF, SPARQL, Python (rdflib, owlready2), JavaScript, Oxigraph

facts: competency questions, each run as SPARQL
project.shows: Testing a model against its own requirements, and reporting what it cannot answer.

decisions.choice: Run every competency question as SPARQL against the group’s OWL files, instead of trusting the documentation.
decisions.why: Competency questions are the requirements an ontology has to answer.
decisions.result: Only 12 of the 24 written queries answered their question as written; fixed and completed, 37 of 47 questions are answered by the files, 7 in part, and 3 ask about things the files do not record.

decisions.choice: Check language-model output against the domain before modelling from it.
decisions.why: ChatGPT and Gemini were used early on for definitions, scenarios and user stories.
decisions.result: It showed where their answers helped and where they had to be corrected.
